_readme: Proofs that cannot run in the test suite, and the hash of what they proved.
cockpit/tests/proof-staleness.test.ts fails while a recorded hash does not
match the file on disk. It does NOT run the SQL and cannot know whether you
really ran it -- it converts 'remember to run this' into 'the suite asks'.
A stale alarm is not a proof. It is the difference between a note and a control.
To bless after running one: npm run proof:bless <id>
`--all` NEVER first-blesses and never re-stamps an unchanged proof. Both were
added on 18 Sep 2026 after a convenience call replaced ten true dates with
today's and stamped two never-run proofs as proved. The first blessing of a
proof is somebody claiming they ran a new thing, and that claim is always
A proof may also be BLOCKED: recorded, exempt from staleness, and carrying
`runnable_when` -- a path that does not exist yet. The moment it does, the
suite fails and says the proof is now runnable and has never been run, and
`proof:bless` refuses it until then. That covers two kinds of deferred
obligation: a proof that cannot be RUN yet, and a check that cannot be
WRITTEN yet. Both are alarms with a trigger rather than a silence.

proofs.what: The views aggregate, group and join correctly. The RULES are proved separately and automatically in cockpit/tests/consent-resolution.test.ts.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0013_consent_view.test.sql into the Supabase SQL editor and run it. It rolls itself back. Expect two NOTICEs and no exception.

proofs.what: The three invariants of the send record and the authorisation freeze, each SEEN to refuse a row it must refuse. Two of the three are check constraints rather than observations, which is only possible because the row precedes the send.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0015_sends_constraints.test.sql into the Supabase SQL editor and run it. It rolls itself back. Expect 'ALL SIX CONSTRAINT CASES FIRED', the neighbour accepted, and three freeze notices. Any 'DID NOT FIRE' is a constraint that is not holding.

proofs.what: The freeze inverted from a denylist to an allowlist: outcome columns writable, every other column frozen INCLUDING ones 0015 never mentioned. 0015's version would have allowed campaign_id to be edited after the fact.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0017_sends_attempts_and_allowlist_freeze.sql, then run its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect: attempts/last_attempt_at/last_error writable; gate_decided_at refused BY NAME; campaign_id refused (0015 would have allowed it).

proofs.what: A halted run must say why, and an evaluated run's counts must add up: target = excluded + permitted + refused. A shape that does not add up is not a record.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0018_campaign_runs.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect halted_states_its_reason to refuse a halt with no reason; forecast_adds_up to refuse 23+20+200 against a target of 300 and to ACCEPT 23+20+257.

proofs.what: The `unresolved` status is accepted where 0015 would have refused it, the freeze still holds on a row in that state, and the two reconciliation indexes exist.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0019_sends_unresolved.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect the unresolved insert to succeed, gate_basis refused by name, reconciled_at/last_error writable, and 2 index rows.

proofs.what: Variable contiguity refused, an approved row without its approval id refused, the body frozen while status stays writable, and a send naming a non-existent approval refused by the new foreign key.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0020_message_templates.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect: contiguity function t/f/t; variables_are_contiguous fires; approved_has_its_approval fires; status update succeeds then body update refused BY NAME; sends_template_approval_fk refuses HX_NOT_REAL.

proofs.what: clients.whatsapp_sender_sid exists and its shape is enforced (XE + 32 hex). Without this column the quality halt cannot read the number it exists to watch.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0021_clients_sender_sid.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect 'not-a-sid' refused by clients_sender_sid_shape and a well-formed XE… accepted.

proofs.what: sends.campaign_run_id exists and its foreign key refuses a run that does not exist. Without it, a run's refusal rows are not attributable to the run, and a second run of the same campaign would read the first's rows as its own.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0022_sends_campaign_run_id.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect the column to exist and an invented campaign_run_id to be refused by the foreign key.

proofs.what: Attribution is a three-state fact: a campaign attribution must name its send, an organic one must name nothing, and — the one that matters — an insert omitting the column entirely (which the live workflow does) inherits `unknown`, the LOUD state, rather than `organic`.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0023_messages_attribution.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect existing rows all 'unknown'; campaign-without-send refused; organic-with-run refused; and an insert omitting attribution_state to SUCCEED returning 'unknown'.

proofs.what: A `declared` event without declared_by is refused; one with it is accepted; and every other kind is untouched — an objection has no declarer, and requiring one would make a contact's own opt-out unrecordable.
proofs.how: Paste db/migrations/0024_declaration_author.sql, then its verify block inside begin/rollback. Expect: declaration without author REFUSED, with author accepted, and an objection with no declared_by accepted.

proofs.what: The two CHECKs that keep a computed match and a chosen one apart, the PARTIAL UNIQUE INDEX (one current row per lead x listing), and the FREEZE (a notified match resists an edit and permits an outcome). The last two need a row that EXISTS and is then changed, which no constraint-only check can reach. Includes the permitted neighbours: a legitimate computed row, a successor once the first is history, and an outcome written after notification -- a table that refused everything would pass every refusal case identically.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0025_listing_matches.test.sql into the Supabase SQL editor and run it. It rolls itself back. Expect 'ALL SEVEN REFUSAL CASES FIRED, and all six permitted cases were accepted'. Any 'DID NOT FIRE' is a guard that is not holding; a MISSING ok on a permitted case is the opposite failure and matters just as much.

proofs.what: An unknown kind is refused rather than stored and never matched (0009's `availabe` in a new place), and an agent's assertion about a lead carries both their words and their name. With the neighbours: a complete agent row, a derived row that needs no author, and area holding a LIST of alternatives in ONE row -- which is lesson 7c, since two rows of an alternatives kind are an AND and match nothing anywhere.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0026_lead_requirements.test.sql into the Supabase SQL editor and run it. It rolls itself back. Expect 'ALL THREE REFUSAL CASES FIRED, and all three permitted cases were accepted'.

proofs.what: THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST IN 0026, AND IT IS NOT A CONSTRAINT. A recompute deletes by source -- field, conversation, note -- and never touches source='agent'. The agent's answer to 'why them?' exists nowhere else and is the only way a name-and-phone list acquires structure. The obvious 'delete every row for this lead and reinsert' destroys it AND LOOKS LIKE IT WORKED, because every derived row comes back.
proofs.how: Given one 'agent' row and three derived rows for a lead, run the recompute and assert the agent row is still present AND carries its ORIGINAL id -- a delete-and-reinsert that happened to write an equivalent row is the same defect with a new primary key. Cannot be run yet: the matching run does not exist.

blocked.reason: The recompute lives in the caller, and the matching run has not been built. There is nothing to run this against.

discharged.note: The rule became provable in the suite rather than in a SQL editor, because the caller was built as a PURE PLANNER: planRecompute() is the only thing that produces ids to delete, so the store applies a plan by id and a delete scoped to the lead cannot be written. Three tests: every derived row is deleted and no agent row; the agent row keeps its ORIGINAL id (a delete-and-reinsert is the same defect with a new primary key); and a lead with only derived rows is fully replaced, so the rule is not 'delete nothing'.

proofs.what: agent_dismissed_lead is a working preference held by an agent, NOT an objection. An objection is permanent, belongs to the contact, lives in the consent ledger, and is recorded because a person asked for it. If the two ever merge, an agent's convenience becomes a permanent legal state on somebody who never asked for it -- invisibly, because both produce the same silence. 0025's header names three safeguards and a migration can only carry two; this is the third.
proofs.how: A source-level boundary check of the kind tests/one-sender.test.ts already does for the provider credential: the gate and its reads -- gate.ts, gate-read.ts, suppression.ts, the consent resolution -- must not import or query listing_matches, and the check must name the offending path rather than return a count. The CANDIDATE-SET query is the one place that SHOULD read it, so the check is a boundary and not a ban. Cannot be written yet: the matching run does not exist, so there is no caller to bound.

blocked.reason: The matching run has not been built, so there is no read path to bound. Recorded now because an obligation recorded and never discharged is worse than one nobody wrote down -- the record proves you knew.

discharged.note: A source-level boundary in both directions: nothing on the gate path reads listing_matches or agent_dismissed, and the matching run does not consult the gate, the ledger or the suppression list. Plus the two tests that stop it becoming vacuous -- every listed file must exist, and the matching side must still read listing_matches, so the boundary cannot be 'fixed' into a ban that blinds the candidate set.

proofs.what: A rating with no expiry date is refused (one we cannot date is one we cannot defend), and an exemption without an author or a basis is refused — because an exemption that is a blank cheque is the door everything walks through and the obligation loses all practical effect. With the neighbours: the same rating WITH a date is accepted, and a complete declaration is accepted. A table that refused everything would pass both refusals identically.
proofs.how: Paste the VERIFY block at the foot of db/migrations/0028_energy_certificate_and_ami.sql into the Supabase SQL editor, inside begin/rollback. Expect: energy_class without a date refused by name; with a date accepted; an exemption missing `basis` refused by name; a complete exemption accepted. Roll it all back.

proofs.what: The stale description of Automation 04 is corrected, and the OTHER FOUR are untouched. A description is what somebody reads when they arrive and want to know what an automation is for; a stale one is how the wrong thing gets built two years from now by somebody who trusted the row. The second half matters as much: an UPDATE whose WHERE clause matched everything would look identical in the first check.
proofs.how: Run 0027, then `select key, left(description,40) from public.automations order by key` and confirm listing_launch carries the new text and the other four are unchanged.

proofs.what: The advertising jurisdiction table: keyed (country, region) with a null region meaning the national row, requirements typed rather than columns, and the PT row RESEARCHED AND NOT CONFIRMED so it permits nothing. Four constraints, each proven by trying to break it — a lower-case country, a region NAME instead of a code, a region row claiming regions_exhaustive, and a confirmation with no author — plus the national row refusing to be duplicated.
proofs.how: Apply db/migrations/0029_advertising_policy.sql, then run its VERIFY block inside begin/rollback. Expect: PT present with confirmed_at NULL and 2 requirements; grants t for service_role and f for anon; each of the four constraint violations by NAME; and the duplicate national row refused. Roll back everything except the PT row.

proofs.what: Four constraints, each with its neighbour: a rating with neither an expiry nor an exemption is refused and the same row WITH an expiry is accepted; an exemption missing its basis is refused and a complete one accepted; a lookup nobody confirmed is not a fact; and an agency status other than 'unknown' must say when it was checked. Plus the region CODE check — a name rather than a code is refused, because Cataluña/Catalunya/Catalonia are three rows for one place.
proofs.how: Apply db/migrations/0030_publication_facts.sql, then run its VERIFY block inside begin/rollback. Every refusal by NAME, and every neighbour accepted — a table that refused everything would pass all the refusals identically. Roll it all back.

proofs.what: The region is a CODE and never a name, and null stays lawful because Portugal does not regulate advertising regionally. The column exists so that adding it later is not adding it to a table with rows.
proofs.how: Apply db/migrations/0031_listing_region.sql, then: set region='CT' (ok), set region='Cataluña' (expect: violates listing_region_code), set region=null (ok). Roll back.

proofs.what: The ONLY destructive migration in the series. It PROVES the five columns are empty before dropping them — a do-block that counts each one and RAISES, naming what it found, rather than a comment asking somebody to check. And the neighbours: the listing and the clients survive with every other column intact, because a migration that dropped too much would pass 'the columns are gone' perfectly.
proofs.how: FIRST prove the abort works, or the guard is a claim nobody has tested: in a transaction you roll back, set clients.ami_licence on one row and run the do-block alone — expect 'REFUSING TO DROP … clients.ami_licence=1 … Nothing has been dropped.' Then rollback, apply db/migrations/0032_drop_flat_publication_columns.sql, and run its VERIFY block: no energy% columns on listings, no ami_licence on clients, and listings/clients row counts and remaining columns unchanged.

proofs.what: The trigger for Automation 05, and the three constraints that carry its design. `close_party_is_whole` — the four party columns are all null or all present, because a party recorded without a declarer is a lawful basis nobody declared, arriving through a side door the segmentation screen exists to close. A close with NO party inserts fine, which is the normal first state and not a degraded one. `close_is_not_in_the_future`. The widened `consent_events.source`, which must accept `close_report` and still refuse anything else — a constraint dropped and re-added is the one place a widening can silently become an opening. And the privileges, which come from 0002's default privileges and are confirmed rather than trusted.
proofs.how: psql: has_table_privilege('service_role','public.closes','INSERT') is t and has_table_privilege('anon','public.closes','SELECT') is f. Then each constraint by TRYING TO BREAK IT, per the migration's own verification block: a party with no declarer expects 23514 on close_party_is_whole; a declarer with no party expects the same; a close with neither inserts cleanly; closed_on = current_date + 1 expects 23514 on close_is_not_in_the_future; party_role = 'landlord' expects 23514; the same (client, listing, day) twice expects a duplicate key on closes_client_listing_day, while two closes with listing_id null both insert because NULLs are distinct; consent_events accepts source = 'close_report' and refuses 'guessed'. Delete the fixtures and confirm zero rows remain.

proofs.what: The host allow-list on `clients.review_link`, which is a POLICY BOUNDARY and not a format check: §8.B is Google's policy, and a link to another platform would run Automation 05 under rules nobody has read. The anchor matters as much as the list — `^https://` must refuse a lookalike host that merely contains a permitted one, and must refuse http. The path is deliberately unconstrained, so the proof must also show a REAL link in two different Google shapes being accepted, or the constraint is tight in a way that rejects what an agency pastes from their own dashboard. And the absence that carries §6.2: no per-sale skip column on `closes`.
proofs.how: psql or the Supabase editor, on a test client, restoring review_link afterwards: 'https://g.page/r/CXyzAbC123/review' and 'https://search.google.com/local/writereview?placeid=ChIJxyz' both update cleanly; 'https://facebook.com/x/reviews' expects 23514 on clients_review_link_is_google; 'https://evil.com/g.page/r/x/review' expects the same refusal, which is what proves the anchor; 'http://g.page/r/x/review' expects the same; null updates cleanly and means the automation does not run. Then: select review_requests_enabled from clients — all true. Then the absence: select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'closes' and column_name ~ 'skip|exclud|disabl|opt_out' — expect zero rows.

proofs.what: The catalogue says what the automations ARE. Three names corrected — 02 and 05 both carried "Referral", a product that is not merely unbuilt but REFUSED (a referred contact has no documented origin, which is segment D, which is what the gate exists to refuse), and 04's name still said "Launch Engine" while 0027 had already corrected that same row's description to a publication gate, so the row disagreed with itself. THE SECOND HALF IS THE PROOF: inbound_concierge and lead_nurture must be UNTOUCHED, and lead_nurture deliberately still reads "Lead Nurture & Listing-Match Drip" — "Drip" names a send that is not built, but the honest replacement depends on which tier the client is on and no document settles a single name, so the migration invents none. An UPDATE whose WHERE clause matched everything looks identical in the first check and is only visible next to the rows it had to leave alone (lesson 7b). SCOPE BOUNDARY, checked and recorded so nobody re-opens it: leads.source is plain text with no CHECK constraint at all — data_type text, udt_name text, nothing mentioning referral — so the value listed in 0001 was a documented convention rather than an enforced one, and nothing there was at risk. It stays: a referred lead who messages us is INBOUND on their own initiative, and what was refused is the automation that takes a name from a client and messages a stranger. Opposite directions of travel. WHY IT IS A PROOF AND NOT A TEST: nothing in cockpit/src reads name or description — every query selects key or id — so no suite can observe this. The first reader will be the redesigned Clients screen, which is exactly why the row had to be true before it is built.
proofs.how: Apply 0035, then read ALL FIVE ROWS TOGETHER rather than the three that changed: `select key, name, left(description, 60) as description from public.automations order by key` — expect db_reactivation 'Database Reactivation', inbound_concierge 'AI Inbound Concierge' (unchanged), lead_nurture 'Lead Nurture & Listing-Match Drip' (unchanged, deliberately), listing_launch 'Publication Gate', reputation_loop 'Post-Close Review Request'. Then the property that motivated the migration: `select key, name, description from public.automations where name ilike '%referral%' or description ilike '%referral%'` — expect ZERO rows. Note the earlier draft of 0035 gave 02 a description containing the word "referral" (to say it is refused) while shipping this exact zero-row check — a check that could not fail for the reason it exists, lesson 1n, arriving inside a migration. The description now says what the automation IS; the refusal and its reasoning live in the migration header and in docs/automation-05-review-request-design.md §1.2, which is where somebody asking "why is there no referral automation" would actually look.

proofs.what: The two monitoring columns 0001 added and nothing ever wrote to — client_automations.health (not null, default 'unknown') and last_run_at (nullable) — are dropped, AND THE ABORT IS SEEN TO FIRE FIRST. They are not merely unused: a column named `health` that always says 'unknown' is a fallback asserting "nobody has checked" (lesson 13), which is true today and stops being true the first time anything writes to it once, at which point every other row still says 'unknown' and now reads as "checked, and fine". §3.17 asks for a per-client health rollup and these are the obvious columns for it to read; §4.7 says derive rather than infer, so the rollup comes from automation_runs, the invariant events and each gate's own refusal instead. THE PART THAT IS NOT 0032 AGAIN: "empty" is a DIFFERENT TEST FOR EACH COLUMN. 0032's five were all nullable, so `is not null` meant somebody put something there. Here `health` is NOT NULL, so `is not null` would match every row and abort always — a guard that fires whatever the truth is. Its predicate is `is distinct from 'unknown'`, written that way rather than <> so it stays correct if the column is ever made nullable. Case 3 of the proof is what distinguishes a correct predicate from a merely present one. AND THE ORDERING: cockpit/src/lib/actions.ts wrote health:'unknown' on insert — the column's own default, written back at it. That line is removed in the same commit and MUST BE DEPLOYED BEFORE the migration runs, or client creation breaks in between, because PostgREST rejects an insert naming a dropped column. A migration that is correct in the database and breaks the one screen that writes to the table is not a correct migration.
proofs.how: FIRST confirm the deploy: create a client in the cockpit and see both rows appear (the deployed build must no longer name `health`). THEN prove the abort, in transactions you roll back, running the do-block on its own — three cases, and case 3 is not optional. (1) `update client_automations set last_run_at = now() where id = (select id from client_automations limit 1)` — expect REFUSING TO DROP … health…=0, last_run_at (not null)=1; rollback. (2) `update client_automations set health = 'healthy' where id = (select id from client_automations limit 1)` — expect REFUSING TO DROP … health (anything other than 'unknown')=1; rollback. (3) run the do-block with NOTHING modified — expect the NOTICE 'Both columns are empty — proven, not assumed' and NO exception. A guard that fires on everything is as useless as one that fires on nothing, and `is not null` on a NOT NULL column would pass (1) and (2) and fail this one. THEN apply 0036 and verify: the two columns gone from information_schema; the remaining seven read back in order (id, client_id, automation_id, enabled, config, n8n_workflow_id, created_at) — `config` above all, because it holds every threshold, area and handoff note in the system; row count unchanged; the unique constraint still in pg_constraint. FINALLY onboard a test client again and delete it, which is the check the ordering section exists for.

proofs.what: clients.rehearsal is added NULLABLE and WITH NO DEFAULT, the two documented rehearsal rows are classified explicitly (ZZ TEST — Cascais Demo by id; Ryvo Test Client by the Twilio sandbox number), and the migration REFUSES BY NAME if any row is left unclassified. There is deliberately no rule for 'everything else': no real client has been signed, so an unmatched row is a row nobody accounted for. WHY: the Overview is the landing and its firsts and counts would otherwise present rehearsal data as the business's history (§5j) — a caption explaining a wrong number is worse than a right number. THE PART THAT IS EASY TO GET WRONG: a guard that also refused when zero rehearsal rows exist would refuse the correct post-go-live state; it was written, then removed, and case 3 is what would have caught it.
proofs.how: In transactions you roll back, running the file's body without its begin/commit. (1) insert a client (id 00000000-0000-0000-0000-0000000c1e37, name 'PROOF FIXTURE — unclassified') — expect REFUSING: 1 client row(s) are not classified … naming it; rollback. (2) update clients set whatsapp_number = '+10000000000' where whatsapp_number = '+14155238886' — a wrong matcher — expect REFUSING … naming "Ryvo Test Client"; rollback. (3) nothing modified — expect NOTICE 'Classified, not assumed: 2 rehearsal, 0 real, 0 undeclared.' and NO exception. THEN apply and verify: every row true or false; column_default null; is_nullable YES; row count unchanged.

proofs.what: clients.rehearsal becomes NOT NULL only after proving (a) no row is null — an undeclared row is refused by name, never defaulted — and (b) the column still has no default, because NOT NULL on a column with a default is satisfied on every undeclared row's behalf and proves nothing. ORDER: 0037 applied, THEN the onboarding that asks the question (a required choice, nothing pre-selected) DEPLOYED and seen to write true/false in the running cockpit, AND the db/tests fixtures declaring rehearsal = true — THEN this. 0036's lesson: the deploy is a precondition, not a companion.
proofs.how: FIRST confirm the deploy: onboard a client in the cockpit and see rehearsal true/false (not null) on its row. THEN in rolled-back transactions, the do-block on its own: (1) insert a client with no rehearsal — expect REFUSING … have rehearsal = NULL … naming it. (2) alter column rehearsal set default false — expect REFUSING … has acquired a default (false). (3) nothing modified — expect the NOTICE and NO exception. THEN apply and verify: is_nullable NO, column_default null; an insert omitting rehearsal fails with a not-null violation (rolled back); onboard and delete a test client.

deploy_precondition.breaks: NOT NULL with no default rejects every insert that does not name the column, so client creation fails on the operator mid-onboarding

proofs.what: clearances is created as the publication gate's own decision, kept — the input publication/recheck.ts has never had. It proves its preconditions rather than assuming them (0032's treatment): the tables it references exist, NOTHING called clearances is already there, and listing_facts still has the three columns the snapshot is assembled from. `satisfied` stores the gate's SatisfiedRequirement[] WHOLE, because recheck.ts records what a lossy copy cost — with only (id, expiry, exemption) it could not tell a rating from a registration. A snapshot, never a pointer: joining to listing_facts instead would compare today with today and find nothing, always. 🔴 notice_sent_at records THAT THE AGENCY WAS TOLD AND NOTHING MORE — never that an advertisement came down; the operator named this as the rule most likely to soften once there is a column to write to.
proofs.how: In transactions you roll back, running the do-block alone: (1) with a relation named clearances present — expect REFUSING: a relation called clearances already exists; rollback. (2) rename listing_facts.valid_until temporarily — expect REFUSING: listing_facts does not have the three columns …; rollback. (3) unmodified — expect NOTICE 'Preconditions proven, not assumed.' and no exception. THEN apply and verify: relrowsecurity is true; has_table_privilege('anon', …, 'SELECT') is false; an insert with satisfied = '[]' violates clearances_snapshot_is_not_empty; two rows for one listing in two countries both insert.
proofs.applied_note: Applied and verified 2026-09-20 by the operator in the Supabase SQL editor, all test transactions rolled back. Confirmed independently from the cockpit afterwards: the relation exists and its columns are exactly the set the writer inserts (id, client_id, listing_id, country, region, satisfied, decided_at, notice_sent_at, created_at); listings.country exists, with listings.region read as a control that the probe itself works. ⚠️ The operator’s report named clearance_country_iso, clearance_satisfied_is_a_list and a clearances_current index; this migration names them clearances_country_iso, clearances_snapshot_is_not_empty and the unique constraint clearances_one_per_listing_jurisdiction. The substance checked out and the names did not, so they are recorded here rather than left for somebody to grep for and not find.

proofs.what: listings.country is added NULLABLE and WITH NO DEFAULT, constrained to ISO-3166 alpha-2. 0031 added the region and not the country, and nothing noticed for a month: decidePublication takes a country and NOTHING in the database held one — not on listings, not on clients, nowhere. The gate was complete, correct, and unable to be asked a question it could answer. 🔴 It is entered by a person and never derived: clients.timezone is where the agency's day starts, listings.area is a town name ("Valencia" is a province in Spain and a town in three other countries), and agency_facts.country is where the AGENCY is registered. Each would be the string match that produces a legal conclusion, which is what 0031 refuses. NO DEFAULT, because a default asserts a jurisdiction for every property nobody has looked at.
proofs.how: In transactions you roll back, running the do-block alone: (1) with listings.country already present — expect REFUSING: listings.country already exists; rollback. (2) rename listings.region temporarily — expect REFUSING: listings.region is missing, so 0031 has not been applied; rollback. (3) unmodified — expect NOTICE 'Preconditions proven, not assumed.' THEN apply and verify: is_nullable YES and column_default null; update one row to 'Portugal' violates listing_country_iso; update to 'PT' is accepted.
proofs.applied_note: Applied and verified 2026-09-20 by the operator in the Supabase SQL editor, all test transactions rolled back. Confirmed independently from the cockpit afterwards: the relation exists and its columns are exactly the set the writer inserts (id, client_id, listing_id, country, region, satisfied, decided_at, notice_sent_at, created_at); listings.country exists, with listings.region read as a control that the probe itself works. ⚠️ The operator’s report named clearance_country_iso, clearance_satisfied_is_a_list and a clearances_current index; this migration names them clearances_country_iso, clearances_snapshot_is_not_empty and the unique constraint clearances_one_per_listing_jurisdiction. The substance checked out and the names did not, so they are recorded here rather than left for somebody to grep for and not find.

proofs.what: client_contracts becomes append-only: UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE refused by trigger AND by revoke; supersedes_id added so a correction is a new row; a unique partial index refuses TWO rows superseding the same contract (both would be current and the month counted twice); a row cannot supersede itself; and client_contracts_uncorrected returns only uncorrected rows. WHY: with an editable table, 'what did we earn in January' has a different answer depending on when you ask and nothing records that it changed — the stale-record failure on the page whose entire subject is the past. Same shape as consent_events (0012) and the sends freeze (0017); the pattern is reused, not redesigned. THE PART EASY TO GET WRONG: a freeze that blocks superseding as well as editing makes the table READ-ONLY, and every refusal case still passes — case 5 is the only one that catches it. THE NAME: the view is _uncorrected, never _current — 'current' reads equally as 'not superseded' and as 'covering today's date', and a caller taking the second meaning and summing it for January gets rows in force TODAY: a wrong figure that looks entirely right.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0042_client_contracts_append_only.test.sql. Six cases, each applying 0042 inside its own transaction and rolling back; nothing survives. Expect: (1) UPDATE refused by name, (2) DELETE refused, (3) duplicate key on client_contracts_one_correction_each, (4) contract_supersedes_another on a self-reference, (5) NOTICE 'Correction accepted: 2 rows, 1 current, monthly 450.00' and NO exception, (6) NOTICE 'The overlap check sees a genuine double-count'. If case 5 raises, DO NOT APPLY. THEN apply and verify: service_role holds INSERT and SELECT only; client_contracts_uncorrected returns 0; both supersedes indexes present.

proofs.what: payments.received_on is dropped, leaving settled_on as the only column recording that money arrived. WHY: two columns meaning the same fact eventually disagree, and the one that disagrees is the one somebody trusted — here it would be The Month's `paid` figure, on the page the operator trusts most. settled_on is the survivor because it carries the comment defining the fact and belongs to a model that also expresses a PART payment (settled_amount_eur) and a WRITE-OFF (written_off_on), neither of which received_on can express. Nothing in the cockpit reads received_on — verified by grep, not assumed. THE PART EASY TO GET WRONG: case 2, which refuses to drop received_on when settled_on is absent — otherwise this migration becomes a way to delete the only record that money arrived rather than a duplicate of it. 🔴 STATUS: applied, and the destructive guard is UNPROVEN. Case 2 is the check that stops this file becoming a way to delete the only record that money arrived rather than a duplicate of it, and it has never been seen to fire.
proofs.how: 🔴 0044 WAS APPLIED BEFORE THIS PROOF WAS RUN, so cases 1 and 3 are moot and CASE 2 IS UNPROVEN: by the time it was attempted, received_on was already gone, the migration refused at its FIRST guard, and the second was never reached. It failed for the wrong reason, which is the same as not being tested. Run the 'CASE 2, AFTER THE FACT' section at the foot of db/tests/0044_drop_payments_received_on.test.sql: it adds received_on back and drops settled_on CASCADE inside a transaction, so the first guard passes and the second is reached, then rolls back and VERIFIES the rollback restored settled_on. Expect 'REFUSING: payments.settled_on does not exist…' — and if it says 'received_on does not exist' instead, the reconstruction did not apply and the case is still un-run. Bless only after that refusal has been SEEN.

proofs.what: client_contracts_uncorrected is made security_invoker and stripped of every write privilege. WHY: it is a simple SELECT over one table, so Postgres makes it AUTOMATICALLY UPDATABLE — and for such a view, rights on the underlying table are checked as the VIEW'S OWNER rather than as the caller. So 0042's `revoke update, delete, truncate on client_contracts from service_role` does not govern writes routed through it. The trigger still fires, because triggers live on the base table, so append-only is enforced BY THE TRIGGER ALONE. That is precisely the arrangement 0012 refused: 'the trigger is the guarantee, the revoke is the belt', and a belt with a hole is not a belt. The hole was introduced by the view added in 0042 to make the freeze safer to read.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0045_uncorrected_view_is_read_only.test.sql. Three cases, each rolled back. Case 1 demonstrates the hole BEFORE the fix — an UPDATE through the view — and 🔴 READ WHICH ERROR IT IS: if it names the append-only trigger, the write reached the base table and only the guarantee caught it; if it says 'permission denied for view', the belt already held and 0045 is belt-and-braces. Either way apply it. A sentinel fires if the UPDATE is ACCEPTED, which would mean the freeze is not holding at all. Case 2 asserts no write privilege survives on the view. Case 3 is the resting state: the view must still return exactly one uncorrected row at 450.00 — a view locked down so hard it stops answering is a fix that removes the thing it was protecting.

proofs.what: The write privileges on the five money tables, set deliberately rather than inherited. FOUND BY THE GRANT LISTING: all seven relations carried an identical set — service_role with UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on client_contracts, so 0042's revoke was NOT in force and append-only rested on the trigger alone, which is the arrangement 0012 explicitly refused. 🔴 AND anon HELD TRUNCATE: RLS does not cover TRUNCATE — it filters rows for select/insert/update/delete, while truncate is a table-level operation gated only by the privilege, so a role holding it empties the table whatever the policies say. Per table rather than blanket: client_contracts and cost_checks get INSERT/SELECT only (append-only); payments, costs and web_clients keep UPDATE, because settlement arrives weeks after invoicing, a subscription's price genuinely changes, and a client's status changes. DELETE and TRUNCATE go from all five for every role.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0046_money_tables_grants.test.sql. Four cases, each rolled back. Expect: (1) NOTICE no DELETE or TRUNCATE survives anywhere, (2) NOTICE no UPDATE on client_contracts or cost_checks, (3) 🔴 NOTICE the legitimate writes SURVIVE — this is the case not to skip, since a revoke one word too wide leaves a schema nothing can write to and both removal cases still pass, (4) an UPDATE on client_contracts is refused by EITHER the privilege or the trigger, with a sentinel firing if it is accepted. THEN apply and run the verify block: service_role should hold INSERT/SELECT on client_contracts and cost_checks, plus UPDATE on payments, costs and web_clients; anon and authenticated should hold REFERENCES and TRIGGER and NO TRUNCATE.

proofs.what: listing_matches gains a statement-level TRUNCATE trigger and a row-level DELETE trigger for notified matches. WHY: 0025's freeze is `before update … for each row`, and a row trigger cannot guard TRUNCATE — which fires none — so TRUNCATE was unguarded entirely. 0047 revoked the privilege, leaving a BELT WITH NO GUARANTEE, which is the arrangement this project refuses in the other direction: a future default-privileges change can restore a revoked privilege and then nothing stands in the way. 🔒 A SEPARATE FUNCTION, not 0025's: listing_matches_freeze() reads old.agent_notified_at and to_jsonb(new), and a statement trigger has neither, so reusing it would fail with a null-record error that looks like a bug in the guard rather than a guard working. The delete guard refuses only NOTIFIED matches: an unnotified one is working material, recomputed and discarded, and making the table undeletable would turn cleanup into a migration.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0048_listing_matches_truncate_guard.test.sql. Four cases, each rolled back, each with a sentinel that fires if the expected error did NOT happen. Expect: (1) truncate refused, (2) a notified match cannot be deleted, (3) the existing update freeze still refuses — this file adds guards BESIDE it, and if adding them displaced it the update path would be unguarded while cases 1 and 2 still passed, (4) 🔴 NOTICE 'An unnotified match is still deletable.' — the case not to skip, since a guard one condition too wide makes the table undeletable and all three refusals still pass. THEN apply and verify THREE triggers: freeze (update/row), no_delete_notified (delete/row), no_truncate (truncate/statement).

proofs.what: DELETE and TRUNCATE are revoked on listing_matches from every role, and UPDATE is kept for service_role deliberately — retiring a match sets superseded_at, and the trigger is what refuses a change to a NOTIFIED match. A grant cannot make that distinction and must not try. WHY IT EXISTED: 0025 gave the table a freeze trigger and NO revoke, so the belt was never written rather than never applied — invisible to audit_revoke_claims.sql, which compares claims against reality and finds nothing when there is no claim. 🔴 THIS PROOF WAS WRITTEN AFTER THE MIGRATION WAS APPLIED, because it was never written before: 0047 shipped with no proof entry and nothing noticed. cockpit/tests/every-migration-has-a-proof.test.ts now makes that impossible.
proofs.how: Paste db/tests/0047_listing_matches_belt.test.sql. Three cases, each rolled back. Expect: (1) NOTICE no DELETE or TRUNCATE survives, (2) 🔴 NOTICE service_role keeps INSERT, SELECT and UPDATE — the case not to skip, since a revoke one verb too wide takes UPDATE with it and makes the table append-only by accident, which is not what 0025 designed and which case 1 passes either way, (3) `set local role service_role` then a DELETE matching no rows: expect 'permission denied for table listing_matches', with a sentinel firing if it is permitted, which would mean the session is not running as that role and the case is un-run rather than passed.

proofs.what: 🔴 THE CONSENT LEDGER — the record of who may lawfully be messaged, and the table every other freeze in this database was argued from. It predates the proof book by one migration and had never been registered. Proves: service_role holds INSERT and NOT update, delete or truncate (the belt, asked of the database rather than read from the migration, because tonight found a revoke elsewhere that had never applied); the append-only trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE (the guarantee); an unknown kind is refused, since the eight kinds are the vocabulary the gate reads and a ninth would be stored and silently ignored; consent_given with no occurred_at is refused, because consent without a moment cannot be evidenced; a non-E.164 number is refused, because the ledger is keyed on the number and an objection nobody can find protects nobody. AND THE RESTING STATE: a legitimate event must INSERT — six refusals pass just as well on a table that accepts nothing at all. 🔴 CASE 8, added after cases 1-7 passed: the STATEMENT-level truncate trigger had never been exercised. A naive TRUNCATE is refused by the ENGINE first — 'cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint … sends references consent_events' — so today the ledger is protected from truncation by a FOREIGN KEY BELONGING TO ANOTHER FEATURE, incidentally. If sends were dropped, that protection would go with it and nobody would notice, because the guard meant to do the job has never been seen to do it. Same shape as 0044's guard 1 shadowing guard 2, arriving from the engine rather than from a migration.
proofs.how: 🔴 THE ONLY PROOF HERE THAT RUNS AGAINST A LIVE TABLE WITH REAL DATA. Paste db/tests/0012_consent_events.test.sql. It does NOT apply 0012 — that is long applied — it tests the deployed table. Every case is in a transaction and rolls back, and cases 2-6 attempt writes that must be REFUSED, which by definition change nothing. Expect: (1) NOTICE 'Privileges: INSERT t, UPDATE f, DELETE f, TRUNCATE f', (2) UPDATE refused by the trigger, (3) DELETE refused, (4) consent_events_kind_known, (5) consent_events_consent_is_dated, (6) consent_events_phone_e164, (7) 🔴 NOTICE 'The resting state holds' — the case not to skip. Each refusal carries a sentinel that fires if the write was ACCEPTED. A final block verifies no fixture row survives: they are append-only and could not be deleted if one did. 🔴 CASE 8 IS SEPARATE AND MORE DANGEROUS THAN THE REST: run the read-only pg_constraint query above it FIRST to enumerate what references the ledger. It drops ONLY sends_consent_event_id_fkey inside the transaction — not TRUNCATE ... CASCADE, which would put sends at risk too in exactly the failure case being tested — then truncates, expecting the trigger to refuse. It sets lock_timeout and statement_timeout because an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the ledger blocks the Concierge's inbound path, so run it at a quiet moment. A final block verifies the foreign key came back AND reports the row count; if the truncate went through and the rollback failed, the rows are append-only and no statement can restore them — that is a restore-from-backup conversation.
